title: With the legislative session past, all eyes turn to looming primaries
summary: There are no closely fought statewide races to speak of, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t many consequential primaries, with plenty of drama, farther down the ballot.Soon enough, everyday citizens won’t be able to avoid the electioneering.
content:
by Josh Kurtz, Maryland Matters April 22, 2026

by Josh Kurtz, Maryland Matters April 22, 2026

First of two parts

Now that the General Assembly session has ended, Maryland’s political community is turning its full-time attention to the June primaries for federal, state and local offices. Soon enough, everyday citizens won’t be able to avoid the electioneering.

There are no closely-fought statewide races to speak of, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t many consequential primaries, with plenty of drama, farther down the ballot. And voting will start soon enough: Mail-in ballots should start arriving in voters’ homes by mid-May. Early voting is June 11-18. Primary day is June 23.

Another date to circle on the political calendar: May 19, the day the next round of campaign finance reports are due for state and local candidates. These will help reveal the viability of certain candidates – though money is of course by no means determinative in these races.

Congressional candidates just released their quarterly campaign finance statements on April 15; the next round of reports are due out on June 11. Here are some of the most interesting primaries we’re watching this spring.

Four of Maryland’s “Big Eight” jurisdictions have open seat races for county executive where all the consequential action is in the Democratic primary – Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Howard and Montgomery. Harford County is seeing a brutal Republican primary where County Executive Bob Cassilly is trying to fend off two challengers, including County Council President Patrick Vincenti.

One thing that’s notable about the four Democratic primaries is that each includes a strong Black candidate; currently three of the Big Eight jurisdictions have Black leaders. That number could expand this year – though it could also decline, with Howard County Executive Calvin Ball (D) retiring.

Penman wins appeal, reinstatement to seat on Harford County Council

In Anne Arundel, there’s a four-way Democratic primary for county executive. The leading contenders are County Councilmembers Allison Pickard and Pete Smith, and James Kitchin, a top aide to the outgoing executive, Steuart Pittman (D), running with the blessing of his boss.

Pickard enjoys the support of Rep. Sarah Elfreth (D-3rd) and half a dozen powerful state lawmakers. Smith also has his share of lawmaker support, and is trying to consolidate the Black vote in a county with great geographical and economic diversity. To the extent that Anne Arundel’s large military population votes Democratic, Smith, a military veteran, should also have a leg up.

Kitchin is running a less conventional, more reform-minded campaign than his foes, utilizing the county’s brand new public financing system. He received a big boost last month when the Teachers Association of Anne Arundel County threw its endorsement his way.

The primary winner will face Republican Dave Crawford, a retired businessman and volunteer firefighter. In what was until recently a very purple county, the Democrats will be strongly favored to hold the seat.

In Baltimore County, five Democrats want to replace Kathy Klausmeier (D), the outgoing interim executive. The field is led by Councilmembers Julian Jones, Izzy Patoka and Pat Young, along with lawyer Nick Stewart, a former county school board member.

Patoka and Jones are longtime insiders with distinct bases of support. If Jones can get most Black voters to support him, that alone could put him close to victory – and he’s also a favorite of many powerful developers, which makes him formidable. Patoka recently won the teachers’ union endorsement. Stewart’s outsider message is winning him plaudits in certain influential corners of the primary electorate. But he shares a geographic base with Young – which could prove problematic for both of them.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

Pat Dyer and Kim Stansbury are competing in the Republican primary, but the GOP nominee will be the heavy underdog in November. A Republican was last elected Baltimore County executive in 1990.

In Howard County, former Del. Vanessa Atterbeary (D) is seen as the slight favorite to replace Ball. But don’t count out County Councilmembers Liz Walsh (D) and Deb Jung (D), reformers with devoted followings.

Atterbeary, who has a significant portion of the county’s Democratic establishment behind her, plus the endorsement of the teachers’ union, would make history as the first Black woman to serve as Howard County executive. She is also ahead in the money chase, with Jung and Walsh opting to participate in the county’s new public financing system.

Walsh’s campaign recently released a poll showing a wide-open race, with more than half the Democratic primary voters labeling themselves as undecided. After the initial query, Atterbeary had 17%, Walsh had 13% and Jung had 12%. But when Walsh’s pollster offered respondents positive descriptions of the candidates, Walsh surged 4 points ahead of Atterbeary. The poll of 401 likely Democratic primary voters was taken April 6-9 by Hart Research Associates and had a 5-point margin of error.

“The election for Howard County Executive is THE DEFINITION of a fluid and up-for-grabs race,” Hart Research wrote in a polling memo.

Republicans, who held the Howard County seat as recently as 2018, couldn’t even find a candidate to run for executive this year.

Democratic candidates for Montgomery County’s top job make pitches at forum

In Montgomery County, five Democrats are bidding to replace term-limited County Executive Marc Elrich (D), with Councilmembers Andrew Friedson, Evan Glass and Will Jawando – all ambitious 40-something lawmakers finishing their second terms – the frontrunners.

Friedson is a prodigious fundraiser with the development and real estate community squarely behind him, and he may pick up additional firepower from a supportive super PAC that is rumored to be in formation.

Jawando and Glass are participating in the county’s public financing system, as Elrich did during his two victories for county executive; they’ll have more spending restrictions placed on them as a result.

But Jawando has endorsements from several important groups that can provide boots on the ground, including the teachers’ union, Service Employees International Union, and CASA, the immigrants’ rights organization. Glass has the backing of the Sierra Club. Friedson has been endorsed by the unions for both the professional and volunteer firefighters, and, to counter Jawando’s teachers’ backing, the Montgomery County Public Schools Retirees Association.

The only publicly released poll on the primary came from Glass’ camp and was taken two months ago. It showed him with 21%, Jawando with 20%, and Friedson with 16%. Glass and Jawando are at-large council members representing the entire county, while Friedson represents a single district, so he is less well known to the broader electorate than his foes. The poll of 400 likely voters, conducted Feb. 9-12 by Impact Research, had a 4.9-point margin of error.

In Harford County, the incumbent county executive, Cassilly, is seeking a second term, but he is facing a tough GOP primary challenge from Vincenti, the County Council president. The race seems to be more about personalities and factions within the county GOP than substantive differences between the candidates – though Vincenti is more of an old-style “Main Street” Republican while Cassilly has a harder conservative edge.

Vincenti’s support from the teachers’ union and his campaign contributions to Democrats on the County Council are sure to emerge as discussion points in the GOP primary. But there are plenty of political crosscurrents at work, and there are tough down-ballot Republican primaries that reflect these schisms.

The GOP primary to replace Vincenti as council president is equally hot. It’s between Billy Boniface, a one-time top aide to former Harford County Executive Barry Glassman (R), and Councilmember Tony “G” Giangiordano. Ditto the GOP primary for sheriff, where the incumbent, Jeff Gahler, is being challenged by Keith Runk, a former Secret Service officer and Cassilly ally.

Democrats will be heavy underdogs in the general election for these offices.

Millions already raised, spent on handful of Maryland congressional primaries

It’s the moment they’ve all been waiting for: A 24-way Democratic primary is happening in the congressional 5th District, where Rep. Steny Hoyer (D) is retiring after 45 years in the job. Such huge candidate pile-ups aren’t that unusual when a longtime officeholder moves on: 22 Democrats ran in the 3rd District when then-Rep. John Sarbanes (D) decided to call it a career.

But this race is considerably harder to read. It features six current or former elected officials; a former Capitol Hill police officer who has been a high-profile defender of democracy since the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection; a free-spending businesswoman making her second run for the seat; and several candidates who have been campaigning since well before Hoyer announced his retirement.

The only publicly released poll came from former Prince George’s County Executive Rushern Baker (D), which showed him well ahead of the field, with former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn, the runnerup in the 3rd District primary in 2024, in second place, and County Councilmember Wala Blegay third. Everyone else was pretty far behind.

Baker’s poll reflects his high name recognition: He’s been on the countywide or statewide primary ballot in 2002, 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2025. But he’s never been a very aggressive fundraiser.

Dunn has reported raising about $2 million so far. Quincy Bareebe, the CEO of a home health care business, has put at least $3 million of her own money into the race. She began mailing literature early and is now running TV and digital ads.

The current elected officials in the Democratic primary are Blegay, who is backed by Prince George’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy (D) and several of her fellow council members; Del. Adrian Boafo (D-Prince George’s), who has Hoyer’s valuable endorsement; Charles County Commission President Reuben Collins III (D); state Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles); and Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s).

Dunn and Baker seem like they’ll be major contenders to the end, despite obvious weaknesses. Boafo, by virtue of his association with Hoyer, is also likely to be in the hunt all the way. He’ll no doubt benefit from a barrage of ads featuring the venerable incumbent.

One big question is whether AIPAC, the deep-pocketed pro-Israel group, begins investing in the primary on Boafo’s behalf. That could make a huge difference if the race remains close – even though AIPAC is less popular in Democratic circles these days than it was in the past two election cycles, when it spent $4 million on two separate congressional elections in Maryland.

This Democratic race is going to be close through the primary. The victor will then be heavily favored over the winner of a three-way Republican primary.

Two other congressional races rate a mention. In the 6th District, eight Democrats are running but the race is expected to be between freshman Rep. April McClain Delaney (D) who is trying to fend off an intra-party primary challenge from the man who gave up the seat two years ago, former Rep. David Trone (D).

Spending will be other-worldly, especially from Trone, who dropped $62 million of his own money during his unsuccessful run for U.S. Senate two years ago. McClain Delaney and Trone will skirmish over a few issues and over who provided the district with better constituent services. But in the end, the outcome of the primary is not likely to impact the battle for control of the U.S. House – even in what is considered the most competitive congressional district in Maryland.

Republicans will decide among Marine Corps veteran Chris Burnett, frequent candidate Robin Ficker, and Mariela Roca, a military veteran and medical logistics specialist who has already sought the GOP nomination twice.

In the Baltimore-based 7th District, seasoned U.S. Rep. Kweisi Mfume (D) faces an aggressive, credible primary challenge from Baltimore City Councilmember Mark Conway (D), who is making a generational and ideological appeal. It seems inconceivable that Mfume could lose – but Conway is an appealing challenger and stranger things have happened. Yet Conway is slipping on the fundraising front, suggesting he hasn’t built the momentum he needs to topple the popular incumbent.

Next: Legislative primaries and more local races to watch.
